title: The Memoir That Kept Disappearing: Louis-le-Grand, Sainte-Pélagie, and the Pond at La Glacière
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bourg-la-Reine, birth in the pension house
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth on 25 October 1811 at Bourg-la-Reine, then in the departement de la Seine, per Encyclopedia.com and MacTutor; Dupuy (1896) has the birth act declared the next day, which fixes the town against a later tradition that placed him vaguely in Paris. Coordinates corrected: the research pool carried 48.7761, 2.3021, which falls about a kilometre west of the commune toward Sceaux. The commune's own point is 48 deg 46 min 47 sec N, 2 deg 18 min 54 sec E, and this pin places the Grande Rue on the axis of today's avenue du General-Leclerc.
stops.campa: A son is born in the pension house on the Grand'Rue, the boarding school his father Nicolas-Gabriel Galois directs and where his mother Adélaïde-Marie Demante, daughter of a magistrate, keeps the household. They declare him the next day as Évariste. He is the second of three: Nathalie-Théodore came in 1808, Alfred will come in 1814. Nothing in the house is mathematical. The town sits on the road south out of Paris, close enough that the capital's quarrels arrive with the day's post, far enough that a schoolmaster can be the most respected man in it.
suggested_refs: The birth act of 26 October 1811 in the registers of Bourg-la-Reine
The site of the Galois pension on the Grande Rue, today the avenue du Général-Leclerc
sources: Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois
MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Bourg-la-Reine, the father in the mairie
stops.date_confidence: the office is attested, the year is not. Encyclopedia.com names Nicolas-Gabriel Galois as director of the family pension and later mayor of Bourg-la-Reine; no source reached here gives the date of his election, and 1815 is an ordering device only. The defamation campaign that ends his life in 1829 is attested by Encyclopedia.com and Dupuy; nothing found dates its beginning.
stops.campa: Nicolas-Gabriel Galois becomes mayor of Bourg-la-Reine, a liberal running a commune that has been royalist since before the Revolution. He directs the pension and the town at once, writes verses for local occasions, and is well liked by the people who elected him. His second son is three. A schoolmaster who is also a mayor occupies a position that can be attacked from the pulpit and from the prefecture in the same week, and in this town it eventually is. The forged verses and the campaign that kill him are fourteen years off.
suggested_refs: The mairie of Bourg-la-Reine under the Restoration
sources: Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois
Paul Dupuy, La vie d'Évariste Galois (1896), via fr.wikisource.org

stops.name: Bourg-la-Reine, the mother's lessons
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline, undated in detail. Encyclopedia.com and MacTutor agree that Adelaide-Marie Demante taught him at home in Latin, Greek, French letters and Christian instruction until secondary school, and that no childhood mathematical precocity appears in any record. The year 1817 is an ordering device inside the 1811-1823 span; no source reached fixes when the lessons began or ended.
stops.campa: His mother teaches him herself, and there is no school before her. Latin, Greek, the French moralists, religion, the whole classical discipline of a family of jurists laid out for a boy who will not sit in a classroom until he is twelve. What the house gives him is a training in reading fast and holding a position. No contemporary record shows a child prodigy at numbers in these years, and none of his teachers later claims to have seen one. Whether anyone in the pension noticed anything unusual about the boy at all, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Demante family of jurists, from whom his mother's classical education came
sources: Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois
MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Collège royal Louis-le-Grand, entry as a boarder
stops.date_confidence: contested, and not resolved here. MacTutor dates the entry to 6 October 1823 and Encyclopedia.com gives October 1823; Caroline Ehrhardt's archival work in the school registers places formal registration in February 1824 and entry into quatrieme on 1 April 1824. Both datings are in print and the conflict is documented, not adjudicated. Coordinates corrected: Louis-le-Grand at 123 rue Saint-Jacques is 48 deg 50 min 53 sec N, 2 deg 20 min 40 sec E; the pool's 48.8464 sat roughly 190 m too far south, near the rue Cujas.
stops.campa: He goes up to Paris at twelve and into the Collège royal Louis-le-Grand as a boarder in the fourth class, on the rue Saint-Jacques, in a school run with the discipline of a barracks and with the Revolution still in the memory of its walls. The pension at Bourg-la-Reine, where his father was the authority and his mother the teacher, ends for him in a single afternoon. He will live inside this building for the next six years. Boarders rise before dawn, eat badly, and are let out of the walls rarely.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Collège royal Louis-le-Grand, 1823-1824, as read by Caroline Ehrhardt
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois
Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Louis-le-Grand, the year of the expulsions
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline by MacTutor, which records a wave of pupil expulsions at Louis-le-Grand in 1824 over resistance to the school's authority, and that Galois was neither among the leaders nor expelled. The occasion, the number of boys put out, and the month are given by no source reached; the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A wave of expulsions goes through Louis-le-Grand, pupils turned out of the building over resistance to the school's authority, and the year is remembered afterward as the year the college moved against its own. Galois is not among the leaders and keeps his place. He is twelve, in his first year as a boarder. What the occasion was, how many boys were put out, and on whose order, no record reached says. His own reports for the year describe a conventional and successful pupil in the classical stream.
suggested_refs: The disciplinary records of Louis-le-Grand for 1824
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Louis-le-Grand, prizes in Latin verse and Greek
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor, which records prizes and accessits in Latin verse and Greek translation across 1824-1826, including recognition at the Concours general. The individual prizes and their years are not itemised in any source reached, and the date shown is an ordering device inside that span.
stops.campa: He takes prizes and accessits in Latin verse and in Greek translation, and is entered for the Concours général, the competition that ranks the best pupils in France against one another. His mother's curriculum holds: the grammar, the metres, the moralists. The boy incapable of ordinary schoolwork is a figure invented much later, by writers who needed the ruin to have started early. Against them stand three years of prize lists. In class he is orderly and quick, and the reports say so.
suggested_refs: The Concours général prize lists of the mid-1820s
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Louis-le-Grand, sent back down to seconde
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the collapse of his results in seconde, the headmaster's judgement that he was immature and should be held back, the family's resistance, entry into rhetoric in 1826 and the return to seconde after a single term, and the teacher's note 'bon, mais singulier'. Month and day are an ordering device.
stops.campa: His results collapse in seconde. The headmaster calls him immature and wants him kept back a year; the family pushes against it, he goes up into rhetoric, and after one term he is sent back down to seconde in front of everyone. He is fourteen, returned to a class he had already finished, with the classical training that has carried him since infancy no longer carrying him. The mathematics class is the one part of the timetable he has never entered. A teacher writes of him: bon, mais singulier.
suggested_refs: The Louis-le-Grand class reports of 1826, quoted by Dupuy (1896)
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Louis-le-Grand, Legendre read like a novel
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: entry into the mathematiques class under Hippolyte Vernier in February 1827, Vernier's report 'Intelligence, marked progress but not enough method', and the director of studies' report quoted here. The reading of Legendre and Lagrange and the recollection by his classmate Ludovic Lalanne come from the same page, which draws on Dupuy's 1896 life; Dupuy's text was not opened directly in the research pass.
stops.campa: He is put into the mathematics class under Hippolyte Vernier and reads Legendre's Éléments de géométrie the way another boy reads a novel, then goes straight on into Lagrange without waiting for anyone to set it. A classmate, Ludovic Lalanne, remembers the intensity of it years afterward. Vernier praises the ability and objects to the method, and that sentence, ability granted and method refused, is the one every examiner will pass on him for the rest of his life. The director of studies writes to the family that the boy should be allowed to study nothing else.
stops.quote: It is the passion for mathematics which dominates him, I think it would be best for him if his parents would allow him to study nothing but this, he is wasting his time here and does nothing but torment his teachers and overwhelm himself with punishments.
stops.quote_source: Director of studies at the Collège royal Louis-le-Grand, school report, quoted in the MacTutor biography of Galois
suggested_refs: Legendre, Éléments de géométrie, the book he read straight through
Vernier's school reports on Galois, printed by Dupuy (1896)

stops.name: École polytechnique, the first refusal
stops.date_confidence: the failure is attested by MacTutor and Encyclopedia.com; the month is not fixed and 1 August is an ordering device. The surrounding detail is tagged R in the research pool: the story of a chalk rag thrown at an examiner attaches to this failure or to the second one, is oral tradition first written down decades afterward, and the examiner is named in no source reached. Coordinates are the old Polytechnique site on the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve, rue Descartes.
stops.campa: He sits the entrance examination for the École polytechnique, the school that trains the engineers and the artillery officers of France and the one place in the country where his subject is taken seriously, and he fails it. What is documented is the result. The oral record that would explain it has not survived, and the sources disagree even on the month. The story that he threw a chalk rag at an examiner belongs to this attempt or to the next, and it was written down long afterward by nobody who was in the room. Who examined him, and on what, nobody now can say.
suggested_refs: The old École polytechnique on the rue Descartes, Montagne Sainte-Geneviève
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois
Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Louis-le-Grand, the class of mathématiques spéciales
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and by the research dossier's citation of Richard's surviving school reports: entry into the classe de mathematiques speciales under Louis-Paul-Emile Richard in autumn 1828, Richard's judgement of a 'superiorite marquee sur tous ses condisciples', his preservation of Galois's exercises, and a physics report of 'travail nul' in the same year. Month is attested to the term, day defaulted.
stops.campa: Returned to Louis-le-Grand after the refusal, he enters the class of mathématiques spéciales under Louis-Paul-Émile Richard, who reports a marked superiority over every other pupil in the room and says the boy works only in the highest reaches of the subject. Richard keeps the exercises Galois hands him, and they survive, legible and complete, set down in a hand another man can follow. The legend of a mind that could not write out its own solutions has to be argued past them. The physics report for the same year reads travail nul.
stops.quote: This student works only in the highest realms of mathematics.
stops.quote_source: Louis-Paul-Émile Richard, school report, quoted in the MacTutor biography of Galois
suggested_refs: Richard's preserved copies of Galois's classroom exercises

stops.name: Louis-le-Grand, the first published theorem
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: 'Demonstration d'un theoreme sur les fractions continues periodiques' published in April 1829 in Gergonne's Annales de mathematiques pures et appliquees. Day defaulted. The journal was produced in the Midi and not in Paris; the pin is Louis-le-Grand, where Galois himself was sitting, not the place of printing.
stops.campa: His first paper appears in Gergonne's Annales de mathématiques pures et appliquées, a demonstration of a theorem on periodic continued fractions, written by a schoolboy still sitting in a classroom on the rue Saint-Jacques. It is a competent piece of work in a respected journal and it is not what he cares about. In the same months he is building something else: a criterion for deciding when an equation can be solved by radicals at all, and which equations cannot. That work is printed nowhere in his lifetime. He is seventeen.
suggested_refs: Gergonne's Annales de mathématiques pures et appliquées, April 1829
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Institut de France, the memoirs given to Cauchy and Poinsot
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor for the submission, the referees and the loss, with the two dates of 25 May and 1 June 1829. Rene Taton's 1971 reconstruction of the Academy registers, which suggests Cauchy engaged seriously and that Galois himself withdrew the papers to rework them for the Grand Prix, is cited here at second hand through MacTutor and standard modern accounts and was not opened directly. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from joseph_fourier.journey.json, which pins the Palais de l'Institut on the quai Conti at 48.8566, 2.3376.
stops.campa: He sends the Académie des sciences two memoirs on the algebraic solution of equations, on the twenty-fifth of May and the first of June. Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Louis Poinsot are named to report. The manuscripts are lost, and the loss becomes the first entry in a long indictment of the institution. René Taton, working the Academy's own registers more than a century later, found signs that Cauchy took the papers seriously and that Galois withdrew them himself to rebuild them for the Grand Prix. Neither account can be tested against the papers. There are no papers.
suggested_refs: The procès-verbaux of the Académie des sciences for May and June 1829
René Taton's 1971 reconstruction of the Cauchy referral

stops.name: Rue Jean-de-Beauvais, the father
stops.date_confidence: the fact is attested; the research pool's citation was misattributed and is corrected here. Encyclopedia.com says only 'suicide of his father at the beginning of July', with no date, no method and no street. The date of 2 July 1829 is MacTutor's. The asphyxiation and the address, 'rue Jean-de-Beauvais, a deux pas du college de Louis-le-Grand', are Dupuy, La vie d'Evariste Galois (1896), read here through MacTutor and the pool's transcription of fr.wikisource rather than in the original volume.
stops.campa: A campaign of defamation runs against the mayor of Bourg-la-Reine: obscene verses forged in his name and put into circulation by a clerical faction in the town he governs. Everyone concerned knows he did not write them, and it makes no difference to the campaign. Nicolas-Gabriel Galois takes a room in Paris on the rue Jean-de-Beauvais, two streets from the college where his seventeen-year-old son is boarding. His wife is away. He asphyxiates himself there on the second of July.
suggested_refs: Dupuy, La vie d'Évariste Galois (1896), on the forged verses and the rue Jean-de-Beauvais
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Bourg-la-Reine, the stone thrown at the priest
stops.date_confidence: attested by Dupuy (1896) for the return of the funeral to Bourg-la-Reine and the disturbance near the church, read here through the research pool's transcription of the fr.wikisource text. The day is given by no source reached; 5 July 1829 is an ordering device following the death of 2 July. The stone thrown at the priest is reported rather than documented by any act. The reading of the scene as the origin of his politics is flagged in the pool as later biographers' interpretation and is not adopted here as fact.
stops.campa: The body goes back to Bourg-la-Reine for burial. Near the church a confrontation breaks out over the grave of a man the parish helped to destroy, and the priest is struck by a thrown stone. Évariste stands in the principal mourning party while it happens. Later biographers make this the hinge on which his politics turn, a boy radicalised at his father's funeral by the sight of the clergy hounding a dead liberal. The record gives the sequence of events and nothing beyond it. What the boy in the mourning party made of the afternoon, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The parish church of Bourg-la-Reine and the Galois family grave
sources: Paul Dupuy, La vie d'Évariste Galois (1896), via fr.wikisource.org
Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois

segments.name: The Second Refusal and the Preparatory School

stops.name: École polytechnique, the second refusal
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com and MacTutor as the second and final Polytechnique failure, in 1829; the month is fixed by no source reached and 1 August is an ordering device placed after the father's death of 2 July. Dupuy's inability to establish whether the examiner was Binet or Lefebure de Fourcy is carried from MacTutor.
stops.campa: Weeks after burying his father he sits the Polytechnique examination for the second and last time, and fails again. No third attempt is allowed. He is seventeen. There is no transcript, no mark sheet, no examiner's name, and no account of the questions. The grievance survives in perfect condition; of what happened in the room, nothing survives at all. Sixty years later Dupuy could not even establish which of two men had heard him, Binet or Lefébure de Fourcy.
suggested_refs: Dupuy (1896) on the unidentified examiner of 1829
sources: Encyclopedia.com, biography of Évariste Galois
MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: École préparatoire, admitted on his eighteenth birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a conflict of dates carried rather than resolved. fr.wikipedia gives admission to the Ecole preparatoire on 25 October 1829, his eighteenth birthday; Encyclopedia.com gives November 1829. The pin follows fr.wikipedia and the other reading stands. The examiner Leroy's mark of 8/10 in mathematics with a note of originality and obscurity, and the poor physics oral, are from fr.wikipedia and MacTutor. The school occupied the Collège du Plessis, the annexe of Louis-le-Grand on the rue Saint-Jacques.
stops.campa: Refused twice by Polytechnique, he is admitted near the top of the science intake at the École préparatoire, housed in the Collège du Plessis beside his old school and shortly to be renamed the École normale. It trains secondary schoolmasters, which was his father's profession. He enters on his eighteenth birthday, into the second-best scientific school in France. His examiner Leroy gives him eight out of ten in mathematics and writes down both the originality and the obscurity of what he heard; the physics oral goes badly.
suggested_refs: The Collège du Plessis, rue Saint-Jacques, home of the École préparatoire
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, 'Évariste Galois'

stops.name: Paris, the two examiners of the baccalauréat
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the baccalaureate of 29 December 1829 and both examiners' reports, the mathematics report also reproduced on English Wikipedia. The sequence is odd on its face, the degree falling after the October or November admission to the Ecole preparatoire; no source reached explains it and the oddity is left standing. The examination hall is named by no source reached, and the pin is the canonical Paris point used across the atlas.
stops.campa: He takes the baccalauréat on the twenty-ninth of December and passes. The mathematics examiner writes that he is sometimes obscure in expressing his ideas, but that he is intelligent and shows a remarkable spirit of research. The literature examiner writes that he is the only student who answered poorly, that he knows absolutely nothing, and that having been told beforehand of an extraordinary capacity for mathematics, he was astonished. Both reports are filed on the same eighteen-year-old within the same days. He is already enrolled at the École préparatoire, and no source reached explains why the degree comes after the admission.
stops.quote: This is the only student who has answered me poorly, he knows absolutely nothing. I was told that this student has an extraordinary capacity for mathematics. This astonishes me greatly, for, after his examination, I believed him to have but little intelligence.
stops.quote_source: 1829 baccalaureate literature examiner's report, quoted in the MacTutor biography of Galois
suggested_refs: The paired baccalauréat reports of December 1829, mathematics and literature

stops.name: Institut de France, the memoir given to Fourier
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the reworked memoir on the condition that an equation be solvable by radicals, submitted to the Academie for the Grand Prix in mathematics, received by Joseph Fourier as permanent secretary, Fourier's death before the judging was complete, and the manuscript never found afterward among the competition papers. MacTutor gives February 1830; the research pool notes the submission was probably late February and the day is an ordering device. Fourier's death on 16 May 1830 is fixed independently in joseph_fourier.journey.json, from which these coordinates are inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: He rebuilds the lost work and submits it for the Grand Prix in mathematics. It reaches Joseph Fourier, permanent secretary of the Académie, who takes it into his own keeping. This disappearance is far better documented than the first one, and nothing in it needs malice to explain it: an old man died in his rooms with a boy's paper somewhere in them. Fourier dies on the sixteenth of May, before the judging is finished. The manuscript is never afterward found among the competition papers.
suggested_refs: The Grand Prix in mathematics of 1830 and its surviving competition file
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Paris, three papers in Férussac's Bulletin
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: three short papers in Ferussac's Bulletin des sciences mathematiques, physiques et chimiques in April 1830, including the work later understood as introducing finite fields, afterward called Galois fields. Month attested, day defaulted. The description of what the papers contain uses modern vocabulary; no source reached quotes Galois himself using anything of the kind. The pin is the canonical Paris point, the journal's editorial address not being established here.
stops.campa: Three short papers appear in Férussac's Bulletin des sciences mathématiques, physiques et chimiques. One of them builds an arithmetic inside a finite collection of numbers, closed under its own operations, every element with an inverse, the whole of it a fixed and countable size. In April 1830 nobody has a name for the object; the name it eventually takes is his. He cannot get the Académie to read the work he actually wants read. He is eighteen and printed in a bulletin of abstracts.
suggested_refs: Férussac's Bulletin des sciences mathématiques, physiques et chimiques, April 1830
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: Institut de France, the Grand Prix goes elsewhere
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the Grand Prix in mathematics awarded to Niels Henrik Abel, posthumously, and to Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, and Galois's own candidate memoir lost with Fourier. MacTutor dates his learning of it to June 1830; the day is an ordering device. Abel's death of tuberculosis in April 1829 at twenty-six is standard biography and was not re-verified in this pass. Coordinates inherited from joseph_fourier.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Grand Prix in mathematics goes to Niels Henrik Abel, dead of tuberculosis the year before and honoured posthumously, and to Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi. Abel had proved the general quintic unsolvable and died at twenty-six without a post. Galois hears of the award the way an outsider hears of it, from the announcement. The memoir he wrote for this competition went into Fourier's hands in February and has not been seen since, so there is nothing to withdraw, nothing to appeal, and no paper on the table with his name at the top of it.
suggested_refs: The Académie's Grand Prix in mathematics of 1830, awarded to Abel and Jacobi
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: École préparatoire, locked in during the Trois Glorieuses
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the confinement of the Ecole preparatoire students by the director Guigniault during the July Revolution, Galois's reported attempt to climb the courtyard wall at night, and his later resentment that Polytechnique students had fought openly while his own school was shut, together with the death of the former Normalien Farcy. The wall attempt is reported, not documented. The pin date is the first of the three days of 27-29 July 1830.
stops.campa: Paris rises against the ordinances of Charles X, and Guigniault, director of the École préparatoire, locks his students inside the building for the duration. In the streets he cannot reach, students of the Polytechnique, the school that refused him twice, are fighting in the open, and a former Normalien named Farcy is killed there. Three days later France has a new king and he has had no part in any of it. He carries the grievance for the rest of his life, which is under two years. Galois goes at the courtyard wall in the dark and cannot get over it.
suggested_refs: The Trois Glorieuses of 27-29 July 1830 and the Polytechnique students in the streets
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Évariste Galois

stops.name: École normale, the anonymous letter
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a correction to the research pool. The pool gave 8 December 1830 as the date of formal expulsion and attributed it to Encyclopedia.com; no source reached supports that. fr.wikipedia gives the anonymous letter and Guigniault's riposte on 9 December 1830, with the formal decision ratified on 4 January 1831, and those are the dates carried here. MacTutor attests the letter, the identification of its author and the expulsion without giving a day.
stops.campa: A letter signed Un élève de l'École Normale appears in the Gazette des Écoles attacking Guigniault's conduct during the July days. The director identifies the author and throws him out on the ninth of December; the decision is formally ratified on the fourth of January. Galois is nineteen, thrown out of the school that trains schoolmasters, holding no qualification that permits him to teach and no money at all. Guigniault's own report concedes the pupil's incontestable talent while condemning everything else about him.

stops.name: Caillot's bookshop, the public course in higher algebra
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the announcement on 13 January 1831 of a public course in higher algebra at the bookseller Caillot, 5 rue de la Sorbonne, the syllabus as listed here, and an initial attendance of roughly forty. The falling away of the audience is MacTutor's characterisation. Coordinates are a placement on the rue de la Sorbonne, not a surveyed doorway.
stops.campa: With no school and no post he advertises a public course in higher algebra at the bookseller Caillot's premises, 5 rue de la Sorbonne: a new theory of imaginary quantities, the solvability of equations by radicals, number theory, elliptic functions handled algebraically. Every subject on the handbill is one that nobody in France is teaching, and most of them are his own inventions. It does not turn into a living. About forty people come to the first session, and the room empties out over the weeks that follow.
suggested_refs: The announcement of the course at the bookseller Caillot, 5 rue de la Sorbonne, January 1831

stops.name: Institut de France, the third memoir
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: submission on 17 January 1831 of the 'Memoire sur les conditions de resolubilite des equations par radicaux', written at Poisson's encouragement to state the case more explicitly, with Sylvestre-Francois Lacroix and Simeon-Denis Poisson named as referees. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from joseph_fourier.journey.json.
stops.campa: Poisson has told him to set the case out more explicitly, and he does it: Mémoire sur les conditions de résolubilité des équations par radicaux, handed in on the seventeenth of January. Sylvestre-François Lacroix and Siméon-Denis Poisson are named to report on it. It is the third time the same argument has gone into this building under a different title. The first version went to Cauchy and vanished, the second went to Fourier and vanished. This one comes back out.
suggested_refs: The Mémoire sur les conditions de résolubilité des équations par radicaux, submitted 17 January 1831

stops.name: Paris, the letter that says he is without money
stops.date_confidence: the text is attested verbatim on MacTutor, introduced there as a letter written on 18 April by Sophie Germain to her friend the mathematician Libri, that is Guillaume Libri. MacTutor gives no year: 1831 comes from context, Fourier having died in May 1830 and the expulsion falling in December 1830, and is not stated by the source. MacTutor's text opens with an ellipsis and contains the typo 'expelled form Ecole Normale', silently normalised in the quotation here. No address is given and the pin is the canonical Paris point.
stops.campa: Sophie Germain, who has done mathematics her whole life from outside every institution that produced these examiners, writes to Guillaume Libri that spring about the student Galois. Hers is the only surviving description of him made by a mathematician of standing while he is alive. She is writing about a nineteen-year-old who in eighteen months has lost a father, two examinations, three manuscripts and a school. What she writes is that he is expelled, penniless, impertinent, clever, and going mad.
stops.quote: .. the death of M. Fourier, have been too much for this student Galois who, in spite of his impertinence, showed signs of a clever disposition. All this has done so much that he has been expelled from Ecole Normale. He is without money... They say he will go completely mad. I fear this is true.
stops.quote_source: Sophie Germain to Guillaume Libri, 18 April [1831], quoted in the MacTutor biography of Galois

stops.campa: Some two hundred republicans dine at Les Vendanges de Bourgogne on the rue du Faubourg-du-Temple, celebrating the acquittal of nineteen of their own, former artillerymen of the National Guard. Galois stands up with a glass in one hand and an open knife held in the same hand, and toasts Louis-Philippe. Alexandre Dumas is at the table. What Dumas sees is the king's name spoken over a bare blade, and he does not stay to hear how the sentence ends: he and the men beside him go out through the window into the garden rather than be found in that room.

stops.campa: He is arrested the next morning at his mother's and put into Sainte-Pélagie to wait for trial. The charge is provoking an attempt on the life of the king, and the evidence for it is a toast made in a room of two hundred republicans, half of whom will say under oath that they did not hear how it ended. Where his mother was living that May, nobody since has established. Dupuy gives one sentence and no address: Galois fut arrêté chez sa mère et mis à Sainte-Pélagie en prison préventive.

stops.name: Palais de Justice, acquitted by the assize court
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and Encyclopedia.com: trial before the Seine assize court on 15 June 1831 for publicly provoking an attack on the king, and acquittal. The wording of the toast is tagged R: both MacTutor and English Wikipedia note that the crowd's noise reportedly drowned the end of it, so the conditional comes from the defence's reconstruction in court, not from any transcript of the banquet. Later claims that he was convicted at this trial are wrong.
stops.campa: He goes before the Seine assize court charged with publicly provoking an attack on the king. He denies neither the toast nor the knife. The whole case turns on whether he added a condition, if he ever betrays, and the noise in that room a month before makes it unprovable in either direction. His counsel puts the conditional in his mouth, and the jury takes it. He is nineteen, and he has spent five weeks in prison over a sentence nobody can reconstruct. The deliberation is short and he is acquitted.

stops.campa: Lacroix and Poisson deliver their report on the January memoir. It is not contemptuous. They say they cannot follow it: that the argument is neither clear enough nor developed enough for them to judge whether it is rigorous, and they return the paper instead of publishing it. The general criterion he claims to hold, the rule that decides which equations yield to radicals and which never will, is exactly the thing they say he has not shown them. Twice before, the same argument went into this building and was never seen again. This time it is handed back to him with a reason written down.
stops.quote: His argument is neither sufficiently clear nor sufficiently developed to allow us to judge its rigour.

On the morning of the fourteenth of July the police come here looking for him and he is not in. The building is still standing, and a plaque on it says who lived there.

stops.name: Pont-Neuf, taken in a uniform that no longer exists
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: the arrest near the Pont-Neuf around midday on 14 July 1831, the uniform of the dissolved National Guard artillery, the loaded carbines, pistols and dagger, and Duchatelet's drawing of the king beside a guillotine. Coordinates are the bridge itself.
stops.campa: Around midday he and Ernest Duchâtelet are taken near the Pont-Neuf. Both are wearing the uniform of the artillery of the National Guard, a corps the king dissolved after the trial of its officers, and both are armed: loaded carbines, pistols, a dagger. It is the anniversary of the fall of the Bastille, and wearing the uniform is itself the offence, the unit having been dissolved out from under it. Duchâtelet is carrying a drawing of the king's head next to a guillotine.

stops.name: Sainte-Pélagie, the wine and the words
stops.date_confidence: attested as Raspail's report and not as Galois's own writing; the research pool's original attribution is corrected here. English Wikipedia's framing is explicit: inmates goaded Galois into drinking for the first time, and Francois-Vincent Raspail, a prisoner with him, recorded what he said while drunk in a letter of 25 July. It is not a letter by Galois and not addressed to Auguste Chevalier. The two sentences quoted are one continuous passage there and are given as one. Dupuy warned that Raspail's scene reads as artistically arranged after the fact. MacTutor separately states, for this same date, that Galois attempted suicide with a dagger while drunk; that could not be corroborated in the research pass and is tagged R.
stops.campa: Back inside Sainte-Pélagie, he drinks for the first time in his life, pushed to it by prisoners who find him green and call him Zanetto. François-Vincent Raspail, held in the same prison, writes down on the twenty-fifth of July what the boy says while drunk: that he will die in a duel over a low coquette, that what he lacks is someone to love in spirit only, that he lost his father and nobody replaced him. It is the most quoted passage in the whole life, and Galois did not write a word of it. Dupuy warned that the scene reads as arranged after the event.
stops.quote: And I tell you, I will die in a duel on the occasion of some coquette de bas etage. Why? Because she will invite me to avenge her honor which another has compromised. Do you know what I lack, my friend? I can confide it only to you: it is someone whom I can love and love only in spirit.
stops.quote_source: François-Vincent Raspail, letter of 25 July 1831 reporting Galois's words in Sainte-Pélagie prison, quoted in the English Wikipedia article on Évariste Galois

stops.campa: The correctional court gives him six months for the uniform and the weapons. He turns twenty two days later, inside. He serves the sentence among the political prisoners of Sainte-Pélagie, where the speeches and the songs and the arguments make a subculture the guards mostly let alone. His sister Nathalie visits and is frightened by how hollowed out he looks. Somewhere in these months a shot fired from a building next door comes through a window and wounds a man in the room.

stops.name: La Force, nine days nobody has explained
stops.date_confidence: tagged R. The transfer to La Force on 22 January 1832 and the return nine days later come from prison-register documentation reported in the research dossier and were not independently re-verified in the research pass. La Force's location in the Marais, off the rue Saint-Antoine, is standard nineteenth-century Paris topography confirmed here only at secondary level on fr.wikipedia; the coordinates are a placement, not a survey.
stops.campa: The prison registers show him moved from Sainte-Pélagie to La Force in the Marais on the twenty-second of January, and moved back nine days later. No reason is entered against either movement, and nothing else about those nine days survives anywhere. It is one of the very few passages in this life that no biographer has tried to fill in, there being nothing there to fill it with. Two dates in a ledger, in the last winter. Who ordered the transfer, and what he did in the Marais, the record does not say.

stops.campa: Cholera is in Paris and killing by the thousand. On the sixteenth of March, with his sentence running out, Galois is moved from Sainte-Pélagie to a private nursing home on the rue de Lourcine, the maison de santé Faultrier, on grounds of health. In the weeks that follow he becomes entangled with a woman called Stéphanie, whose surname historians are still arguing about. The house has other lodgers in it and is not a cell. It is the first time in nine months he has slept anywhere that is not a prison.

stops.campa: The six months are formally up on the twenty-ninth of April and he is released, on terms that leave him where the transfer put him. He is twenty years old and there is nowhere in particular for him to go. He has one published theorem on continued fractions, three notes in a bulletin of abstracts, a memoir returned to him as unreadable, two manuscripts lost inside the Académie des sciences, no degree that qualifies him to teach, no post, no father, and thirty-one days left.

stops.name: Maison de santé Faultrier, the letters of the twenty-ninth
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com and MacTutor: the letters of 29 May 1832, comprising the address 'a tous les republicains' naming an 'infame coquette' and two dupes, letters to friends saying he was 'provoque par deux patriotes' who acted 'de bonne foi', and the scientific testament to Auguste Chevalier summarising his results on the theory of equations and on elliptic functions. The room is fixed by no source reached; the pin follows the Faultrier house where he had been living since 16 March. The letter texts are read here through MacTutor and the pool's transcription of fr.wikisource. The marginal note 'Je n'ai pas le temps' belongs to manuscripts annotated in this period and is widely miscited as proof that the whole theory was composed in a single final night, which it was not.
stops.campa: In one day he writes to all republicans that he dies the victim of an infamous coquette and of two men she has duped; to friends that he was provoked by two patriots who acted in good faith; and to Auguste Chevalier a summary of everything he has found about the theory of equations and about elliptic functions, annotating and cross-referencing his own manuscripts as he goes. He asks that Jacobi or Gauss be requested publicly to give an opinion, not on whether the theorems are true, but on whether they matter.
stops.quote: Tu prieras publiquement Jacobi ou Gauss de donner leur avis, non sur la vérité, mais sur l'importance des théorèmes. Après cela, il y aura, j'espère, des gens qui trouveront leur profit à déchiffrer tout ce gâchis.

A stranger finds him lying there and takes him toward help by cart.

stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com for the burial on 2 June 1832 in the fosse commune, the coffin carried on foot by friends, the crowd of two to three thousand, the heavy police presence, and the absence of any surviving individual grave. stops.campa: Between two and three thousand people follow the coffin to Montparnasse on the second of June: students, former artillerymen, republican delegations, with the police watching for a rising. The funeral stays calm. The rising comes three days later around a different coffin, General Lamarque's, and writers afterward compressed the two into one event. No stone was ever set over him, and no grave in that cemetery can now be shown to be his. His friends carry the coffin on foot to the fosse commune and put him in the common ground.

stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia dates Joseph Liouville's announcement to the Academie to 4 September 1843, quoting 'dans les papiers d'Evariste Galois, j'ai trouve une solution aussi exacte que profonde de ce beau probleme', and the Numdam record gives the publication as 'Oeuvres mathematiques d'Evariste Galois', Journal de mathematiques pures et appliquees, series 1, vol. 11 (1846), pp. 381-444. stops.campa: The manuscripts Chevalier was given pass, eleven years after the pond, to Joseph Liouville, who reads them through and tells the Académie des sciences that he has found in Galois's papers a solution at once exact and profound. It is the same room that lost the first memoir, lost the second, and sent the third back unpublished. Liouville prints the writings in his own journal in 1846, sixty-four pages of them, and mathematicians in Germany, Italy and England start working out what is inside. In the margin of one demonstration Galois had written that he did not have the time.
stops.quote: There is something to complete in this demonstration. I do not have the time.
